    Chapter 12

    Networking Essentials for Cryptography

    🤔 Your messages are chopped into postcards and passed hand to hand by 10 to 20 strangers in different countries. What can each of them read?

    • ⏱️ ~7 min
    • 📚 9 sections
    • 🎮 3 interactive
    • ⭐ 220 XP
    • 🔑 1 fragment

    To understand HTTPS, VPNs and Wi-Fi security, you need a mental picture of how data actually travels across the internet. This chapter gives you just enough.

    12.1🌐 Packets: the internet is a postal system#

    When you load a web page, your data isn't sent as one continuous stream. It's chopped into small pieces called packets (typically up to about 1,500 bytes each). Each packet is like a postcard with:

    • a destination address (where it's going),
    • a source address (where replies should go),
    • a sequence number (so pieces can be put back in order),
    • and a chunk of the actual data.

    Packets hop through many routers on their way, like letters passing through sorting offices. Different packets may take different routes. The receiving computer reassembles them.

    Here's the security point: every one of those hops can read and modify any packet that isn't protected by cryptography. A typical connection crosses 10 to 20 devices owned by different organizations, in different countries.

    12.2🌐 The layers of networking#

    Networking is organized in layers. Each layer has one job and relies on the layer below it, like a letter (your message) inside an envelope (addressing) inside a mail truck (delivery).

    Layer Its job Postal analogy Examples Cryptography at this layer
    Application What programs say to each other The letter's contents HTTP (web), SMTP (email), DNS, SSH PGP, S/MIME, Signal, DNSSEC, JWTs
    Security (between application and transport) Encrypt and authenticate the conversation Sealing the letter in a tamper-proof envelope TLS TLS, the crypto inside QUIC
    Transport Conversations between specific programs; reliable delivery Registered mail with numbered pages TCP, UDP, QUIC (QUIC has TLS built in)
    Network / Internet Addresses and routing across the world Street addresses and sorting offices IP (IPv4, IPv6) IPsec, WireGuard (VPNs)
    Link / Physical Moving bits over one hop: cable, radio, fiber The mail truck on one road Ethernet, Wi-Fi, 5G WPA2/WPA3, MACsec, cellular encryption

    (You may also see the 7-layer "OSI model" in textbooks. It splits these into finer pieces but describes the same idea.)

    The key question for any security tool is: which layer does it protect, and between which two points?

    • Wi-Fi encryption (WPA2/WPA3) protects only the radio hop between your device and the Wi-Fi router. After the router, it's gone.
    • A VPN protects everything between your device and the VPN server. After the VPN server, it's gone.
    • TLS (HTTPS) protects one application's conversation all the way from your browser to the website's server.
    • End-to-end encryption (Signal, WhatsApp) protects a message all the way from your device to your friend's device, so even the company running the service can't read it.
    ✔ section read

    12.3🌐 Encapsulation: envelopes inside envelopes#

    As data goes down the layers, each layer wraps it in its own header, like nesting envelopes:

    With HTTPS, routers can still read the outer envelopes (IP addresses and ports), because they need them to deliver the packet. Only the innermost part, the actual web request, is encrypted.

    12.4🌐 IP addresses and ports#

    • An IP address identifies a computer on a network, like a building's street address. IPv4 looks like 203.0.113.10; IPv6 looks like 2001:db8:85a3::8a2e:370:7334.
    • A port identifies a specific program on that computer, like an apartment number in the building. Web servers listen on port 443 for HTTPS.

    Ports you'll meet in this guide:

    Port Protocol Protected by crypto?
    80 (TCP) HTTP (web, unencrypted) ❌ No
    443 (TCP, and UDP for HTTP/3) HTTPS ✅ TLS
    22 (TCP) SSH (remote login) ✅ SSH protocol
    53 (UDP/TCP) DNS (name lookups) ❌ No (unless DNSSEC for authenticity)
    853 (TCP) DNS over TLS ✅ TLS
    25, 587, 465 (TCP) SMTP (sending email) ⚠️ Optional TLS (STARTTLS)
    993 (TCP) IMAPS (reading email) ✅ TLS
    500, 4500 (UDP) IPsec VPN key exchange (IKE) ✅ IPsec
    51820 (UDP) WireGuard VPN (default) ✅ WireGuard
    1194 (UDP/TCP) OpenVPN ✅ TLS-based

    Most homes and offices use private IP addresses (like 192.168.1.20) internally, and the router translates them to one public address (this is called NAT, Network Address Translation). That's why many devices can share one internet connection.

    ✔ section read

    12.5🌐 TCP and UDP#

    There are two main ways to send data between programs:

    TCP (Transmission Control Protocol): reliable, ordered delivery. Lost packets are re-sent, and everything arrives in order. Used by the web (HTTP/1.1, HTTP/2), email and SSH. Before sending data, TCP sets up a connection with a three-way handshake:

    That's one full round trip (there and back) before any data flows. Round trips matter because they add delay: from Europe to a server in the US, one round trip takes roughly 80–150 milliseconds. Fewer round trips = faster websites, which is why TLS 1.3 worked hard to cut them.

    UDP (User Datagram Protocol): fire-and-forget. No handshake, no guaranteed delivery or order. Faster and simpler. Used by DNS, video calls, online games, WireGuard and QUIC (the base of HTTP/3).

    ⚖️ Pros & Cons

    TCP vs. UDP

    👍 Situational
    TCP

    Reliable, ordered

    • Retransmits lost packets
    • Simple for apps
    • Handshake round trip
    • Head-of-line blocking
    Best for: HTTP/1.1, HTTP/2, SSH, email
    👍 Situational
    UDP

    Fire-and-forget

    • No handshake; low latency
    • Base for QUIC and WireGuard
    • No delivery or order guarantee
    • Often blocked by strict firewalls
    Best for: DNS, video calls, games, HTTP/3
    ✔ section read

    12.6🌐 DNS: the internet's phone book#

    Computers connect using IP addresses, but people use names like example.com. DNS (Domain Name System) translates names into addresses.

    Traditional DNS has two big security problems:

    • No privacy: queries travel unencrypted, so your internet provider, café Wi-Fi operator or anyone on the path sees every site you look up.
    • No authenticity: an attacker can send fake answers ("bank.com is at my address"). This is called DNS spoofing or cache poisoning.

    HTTPS limits the damage of fake DNS answers: even if you're sent to Mallory's server, Mallory doesn't have a valid certificate for your bank, so the browser shows an error. Chapter 15 covers DNSSEC (authenticity) and DNS over HTTPS/TLS (privacy).

    ✔ section read

    12.7🌐 HTTP: how browsers talk to websites#

    When your browser loads a page, it sends an HTTP request, and the server returns a response:

    The cookie is your login session: whoever presents it is treated as you.

    📜 True story: Firesheep (2010). A browser add-on called Firesheep let anyone on a café Wi-Fi network see other people's unencrypted session cookies for sites like Facebook and Twitter, then log in as them with one click. It caused a public outcry, and within a few years major sites switched to HTTPS everywhere, not just on login pages.

    HTTPS is simply HTTP sent inside a TLS-encrypted connection. Same requests, same responses; nobody on the path can read or change them.

    ✔ section read

    12.8🌐 What others can see, with and without HTTPS#

    Information Plain HTTP HTTPS HTTPS + encrypted DNS + ECH
    Your IP address and the server's IP address 👀 Visible 👀 Visible 👀 Visible
    The website's domain name (bank.example) 👀 Visible 👀 Visible (via DNS and the SNI field) 🔒 Mostly hidden
    The page path (/account/statements?id=77) 👀 Visible 🔒 Hidden 🔒 Hidden
    Page content, forms, passwords 👀 Visible 🔒 Hidden 🔒 Hidden
    Cookies and headers 👀 Visible 🔒 Hidden 🔒 Hidden
    Amount of data and timing 👀 Visible 👀 Visible 👀 Visible
    Can someone modify the page in transit? ⚠️ Yes ❌ No (detected) ❌ No

    To hide the IP addresses as well, you need a VPN (which moves trust to the VPN provider) or Tor.

    12.9Hands-on networking#

    🧪 Try it yourself:

    Terminal
    # Look up a domain's IP address (DNS)
dig +short example.com          # or: nslookup example.com

# See the route your packets take, hop by hop
traceroute example.com          # Windows: tracert example.com

# Check whether a server's HTTPS port is open
nc -vz example.com 443

# Watch a plain HTTP request and response (everything readable)
curl -v http://example.com -o /dev/null

# Watch an HTTPS connection: DNS → TCP → TLS → HTTP
curl -v https://example.com -o /dev/null

    Part of the curl -v https://... output looks like this (lines start with * for connection info):

    To see packets for yourself, install Wireshark, a free tool that shows every packet on your network. Capture while visiting an http:// site and an https:// site, and compare what's readable.
